1. Core Clinical Tension: A 15-year-old adolescent with close dog exposure presented with a 1-month history of feverishness, night sweats, weight loss, cough, expectoration of cystic fluid, and acute pneumothorax with an excavated air-fluid level and mediastinal adenopathy. This presentation closely mimics complicated cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis or a ruptured necrotizing lung abscess, obscuring an unusual primary pleural manifestation of echinococcal disease.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following initial clinical evaluation, physical examination demonstrating a right pneumothorax, admission chest radiography, chest CT defining the hydropneumothorax and cavitary communication, abdominal ultrasound ruling out hepatic lesions, and initial hematology/inflammatory labs, immediately prior to send-out serological testing and thoracotomy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis was strongly considered given chronic fever, night sweats, weight loss, mediastinal/hilar adenopathy, and pneumothorax, but was excluded by positive specific serology and surgical identification of an intact parasitic cyst. Ruptured bacterial lung abscess or empyema was suspected due to productive sputum, fever, and CRP of 165 mg/L, but refuted by the cystic nature of the cavity and surgical extraction of a well-defined larval cyst.
case_prompt:
A 15-year-old student living in a rural agricultural setting with regular contact with domestic dogs presented to the emergency department with acute chest pain and worsening dyspnea. Her symptoms had evolved over the preceding month, characterized by cough productive of yellowish sputum, an episode of sudden expectoration of clear fluid contents, subjective fevers, night sweats, and marked deterioration in general health.

On physical examination, the patient was in respiratory distress. Examination of the chest revealed an air effusion syndrome across the right hemithorax, with hyperresonance to percussion and absent vesicular breath sounds.

Initial emergency chest radiography revealed a massive right pneumothorax with complete pulmonary collapse, alongside a parenchymal excavation containing an air-fluid level. Chest computed tomography confirmed a moderate right pleural and fissure hydropneumothorax communicating with a cavitary air-fluid lesion, accompanied by a small pericardial effusion and right paratracheal and hilar lymphadenopathy measuring up to 15 mm. Abdominal imaging revealed no intra-abdominal cystic localizations. Triage laboratory testing demonstrated microcytic anemia with a hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL, a markedly elevated C-reactive protein of 165 mg/L, and normal renal and hepatic function panels.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Cavitary Pulmonary Tuberculosis with Secondary Pneumothorax
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Subacute presentation with fever, night sweats, general decline, cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level, and prominent mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy strongly pointed to cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis; excluded by targeted serology and intraoperative extraction of an intact parasitic cyst.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: all evolving in the context of feverish sensations, night sweats, and a general decline in condition... Within this hyperclarity was an excavation with a hydroaeric level (Figure 1)... a pericardial effusion, and right laterotracheal and hilar adenopathies measuring 15 mm

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Purulent sputum production, high inflammatory markers (CRP 165 mg/L), and an excavated cavity with hydropneumothorax suggested a ruptured bacterial lung abscess with empyema; however, thoracotomy revealed a well-organized parasitic cyst without suppurative bacterial liquefaction.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: progressive onset of a bronchial syndrome consisting of a cough with yellowish sputum... C-reactive protein (CRP) was 165 mg/l... A frontal chest X-ray revealed a large pneumothorax with a collapsed lung. Within this hyperclarity was an excavation with a hydroaeric level

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Epidemiological canine exposure, expectoration of cystic contents, hydropneumothorax communicating with a fluid cavity, positive hydatid serology (index 6.6), and emergency posterolateral thoracotomy demonstrating a primary pleural hydatid cyst with associated fibrin deposits confirmed ruptured thoracic echinococcosis, treated successfully by complete cyst resection and decortication.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Hydatid serology was positive at 6.6. Treatment consisted of thoracotomy combined with medical therapy. A posterolateral right thoracotomy was performed, revealing a healthy hydatid cyst at the pleural level with fibrin deposits. The cyst was extracted in its entirety, and the fibrin deposits were removed. Pleural decortication was then performed

editor_comments: Distillation completed following Stanford MedCaseReasoning principles. The admission prompt includes epidemiological exposures, exam signs of hydropneumothorax, and initial imaging while strictly removing pathogen and disease identifiers. Reasoning provides verbatim quotes for each differential candidate.
